name: em_inflate
workload: Memory-to-memory decompression of enwik8 (gzip -9 bitstream, 100,000,000 bytes to 36,445,248) and a 32,212,992-byte raw texture file (zlib bitstream, gzip -9 to 13,721,537).
claimed_speedup: enwik8: zlib inflate 1.2.11 426,167 us, em_inflate with checksum 358,118 us (84%), skipping checksum 275,847 us (64%); texture: 127,945 us vs 114,369 us (89%) vs 105,476 us (82%). Derived from page data: about 1.19x and 1.54x on enwik8, 1.12x and 1.21x on the texture file.
tradeoffs: Single file em_inflate.c/.h, single function call, memory-to-memory only: no streaming API, so it is not a drop-in replacement for the zlib inflate stream interface. Needs the whole input and output buffers in memory. Under 1,200 lines including about 300 lines of checksum code. The headline 64% needs checksum verification skipped, which gives up integrity checking.
caveats: First-party README numbers only. CPU model, compiler flags for the timing run, repeat counts and the benchmark harness are not given, and the benchmark code is not in the README. Baseline is zlib 1.2.11 (2017), not a current zlib or zlib-ng/libdeflate, which are much faster than stock zlib at inflate. Commits since 2022 are fixes for buffer overflow and stack usage, so the original timings may predate those fixes. License note: gzip crc32 code from Stephan Brumme is under a zlib-like license, per README. Repo license type taken from README text (zlib license); GitHub page only confirmed a LICENSE file exists. Original that inflatecpp ports.

compiler_and_flags: Workflow: Rust nightly via actions-rust-lang/setup-rust-toolchain, RUSTFLAGS '-C target-feature=+aes', cargo build --release (Cargo.toml: opt-level 3, lto, codegen-units 1, overflow-checks off). Baseline tools are whatever apt installs on ubuntu-latest (versions not pinned).

name: orz
baseline: xz -6, zstd -19/-15/-10, brotli -9/-8/-7, bzip2 -9, gzip -6 (zlib deflate)
workload: Compression and decompression of enwik8 (100 MB Large Text Compression Benchmark file) with each tool's command line; the repo also runs the table in a GitHub Actions workflow (enwik8-benchmark.yml) on ubuntu-latest.
claimed_speedup: orz -l2 compresses enwik8 to 26,892,825 bytes in 3.360 s versus xz -6 26,665,156 bytes in 44.936 s and zstd -19 26,944,223 bytes in 45.985 s (derived from page data: about 13x faster encode than xz -6 at 0.85% larger output). orz -l0: 27,898,433 bytes in 1.773 s versus gzip -6 36,548,933 bytes in 2.441 s (smaller and faster) and zstd -10 30,697,508 bytes in 1.958 s. Decode is slower than zstd and gzip: orz 0.578-0.603 s versus zstd 0.082-0.085 s and gzip -6 0.107 s; xz -6 decodes in 0.812 s.
tradeoffs: ROLZ + move-to-front + static Huffman: strong ratio for text at high compression speed but slow decode compared with zstd, brotli, gzip (about 7x slower than zstd). CPU-feature flag +aes is set in the workflow, which suggests the Rust build is tuned for x86 with AES; portability of the speed claim to other CPUs is untested. Rust nightly toolchain needed (edition 2024).
caveats: Benchmark script is public and the workflow gives compiler and flags, but the CPU model is not stated and baseline tool versions are not pinned (apt on ubuntu-latest), so it falls short of tier A. The README table was produced on an unnamed machine and may not match the Actions output. Single file (enwik8, English text), so ratio claims do not generalize to binary data. Baseline levels chosen are higher-ratio ones: no zlib -9 or lz4 row, gzip -6 is the only deflate row. Not a decode-speed win; the claim is compress speed at matched ratio. Libzling successor by the same author.

name: m77rip
workload: Rust encoder/decoder for the misa77 format; its own benchmark times the first 1 MiB of each of the 12 Silesia files, single thread, best of 10 rounds, against the vendored misa77 C++ reference, not against lz4 or zstd.
claimed_speedup: Only an inherited prose claim that misa77 decompresses '1.5-2x faster than LZ4' with no numbers or setup; m77rip's own table shows decode 4,059-6,641 MB/s (default build, levels -1 to 4, geomean over 12 Silesia files) at 0.87x-0.91x of misa77's C++ speed, ratio 1.955-2.525. No lz4 or zstd throughput appears on the page.
tradeoffs: Memory-safe Rust port of misa77. Default build uses unsafe SIMD; the 'paranoid' build (no unsafe) decodes at 1,038-2,611 MB/s, 0.22x-0.44x of misa77's C++ speed, so safe Rust gives up most of the decode advantage. Encoder is slow (level 4 about 12.9 MB/s, level 1 57.4 MB/s) and needs std and 64-bit; decoder is no_std and 32-bit capable. Write-once, read-many design: trades compression speed for decode speed.
caveats: No numeric comparison against lz4, zstd or any listed baseline in this repo; the only lz4 statement is the unsupported '1.5-2x faster than LZ4' claim about misa77 (origin codec, repo not opened). Own benchmark compares m77rip against misa77's C++ reference and shows it slower on decode in the default build (0.87x-0.91x). Tier D given because no usable baseline numbers; star count is low (7). The bench directory holds a chart generator (bench/src/bin/m77rip_charts.rs) only.

name: fast_zlib
workload: Compression at level 9 of Unreal Engine 4 source code (137 MB), UE4 Win64 binaries, and graphics files (TIF/PNG geometry and textures) up to 256 MB; also the Silesia corpus (202.1 MB).
claimed_speedup: Wiki Release 2, level 9: source code 5.1 s vs 10.7 s for original zlib (same 28.9 MB output); binaries 12.6 s vs 49.1 s (54.5 MB both); geometry 18.2 s vs 180.0 s (114.9 MB both). Wiki states '2.5-10 times faster'. Silesia level 9: 20.90 Mb/s vs 8.51 Mb/s (about 2.5x). Derived from page data: 2.1x, 3.9x and 9.9x on the three sets.
tradeoffs: Replaces only longest_match in deflate.c (C version or 32-bit x86 NASM assembly); zlib 1.2.13+ needs a patch because ASMV was removed upstream. Output format stays standard deflate, so any inflater reads it. Wiki says compressed sizes are equal to original zlib; the README says 'slightly smaller'.
caveats: First-party numbers on an old laptop CPU with MSVC on Windows; the key datasets (UE4 source, binaries, textures) are the author's own and are not published, so the run is not reproducible, and compiler flags are not given. Baseline is zlib 1.2.11 only; no comparison with zlib-ng, libdeflate or Cloudflare/Intel zlib forks. Speedup is largest at level 9 and on poorly compressible data (geometry 180 s original); typical text gains are about 2x. The wiki page text was read through WebFetch summarization; README itself gave no numbers.

name: jtkukunas/zlib (Intel zlib fork)
workload: Compression speed at levels 1, 5/6 and 7-9 on HTML, executables, JPEG and PNG pixel data, as reported by a third-party blog comparing the Intel and Cloudflare zlib forks with stock zlib.
claimed_speedup: Third-party blog snippet only (page blocked): at level 1 Intel's fork takes about 36% of baseline time on an executable; at level 5 about 56% of baseline time on compressible executable data, slower on uncompressible data; faster than baseline at levels 7-9 but slightly behind the Cloudflare fork; decompression much slower than the Cloudflare fork's. Derived: about 2.8x at level 1 and 1.8x at level 5 on executables.
tradeoffs: Fork of zlib adding SSE4.2 crc32 hashing, PCLMULQDQ CRC folding, deflate_quick (level 1) and deflate_medium (levels 4-5). Compression ratio is lower at level 1 (new speed/ratio point) and about equal at level 5. x86 only; archived by Intel with a notice that it is no longer maintained. Repo HEAD is rebased on zlib 1.2.13 per its README and zlib.h.
caveats: The repo README is only the 'PROJECT NOT UNDER ACTIVE MANAGEMENT' notice and has no benchmark. The numbers come from a 2014 blog (Snellman) that this run could not open: egress blocked, so the figures are from a WebSearch result snippet only and were not read in full. The blog measured the 2014 state of the fork, not the later 1.2.13 rebase. Superseded by zlib-ng, which includes deflate_medium and deflate_quick derived from this fork and claims about 4x over stock zlib on x86-64 (search snippet, not opened). Repo license not read from a LICENSE file directly: raw LICENSE and zlib.h carry the standard zlib license text.

name: blz4
workload: Compressed size on the 12 Silesia corpus files using BriefLZ's optimal parser (--optimal) to write LZ4 legacy-format output, compared with lz4 -12 -l and lz4x -9.
claimed_speedup: No speed claim. Sizes are almost identical to lz4: e.g. nci 3,621,482 vs 3,621,567 for lz4 -12 -l; mr 4,190,675 vs 4,190,774; samba 6,100,521 vs 6,100,539; xml 759,868 vs 759,901; most files are byte-identical. blz4 --optimal matches lz4x -9 exactly on every file.
tradeoffs: Produces lz4 legacy-format streams, so lz4 decoders read them. The --optimal mode is described as very slow. Output at best a few hundred bytes smaller than lz4 -12; the decoder is stock lz4, so decode speed is unchanged.
caveats: Not a speed win: the README itself says lz4 'does flexible parsing, is very close to optimal, and much faster', and calls the project 'a quick experiment ... not production quality, and has not been properly tested'. No timings, no compiler, flags, versions or hardware. smallz4 excluded from the table by the author because its output is not the legacy format. Included only because it is a listed niche (optimal-parsing lz4 encoder); the faster-than-baseline criterion is not met.

name: smallz4
workload: Compression of enwik9 (1 GiB) to the lz4 format with optimal parsing, versus lz4 r128 level 9; sizes and times from the author's page as quoted in a search snippet.
claimed_speedup: No compression-speed win. Snippet of the author's page: lz4 r128 -9 gives 374,905,570 bytes in 33 s; smallz4 0.5 -9 gives 371,681,075 bytes in 242 s (derived: output 0.86% smaller, about 7x slower to compress). Newer versions: smallz4 1.5 -9 371,680,328 bytes versus lz4ultra 1.3.0 (favor ratio) 371,680,323 bytes. Decoding uses ordinary lz4, speed unchanged.
tradeoffs: Optimal-parse lz4 encoder (smallz4.h library plus smallz4cat.c decoder). Output is valid lz4, but compression is far slower than lz4 -9 for a roughly 1% size gain. Produces lz4 frame format (not legacy) per blz4's README.
caveats: Numbers come from a WebSearch snippet of the author's site (create.stephan-brumme.com), which is egress-blocked, so the page was not opened and the machine, CPU and compiler are unknown. The GitHub readme is two lines and points to that site; the repo page has no benchmark. The enwik9 figures are older release versions (0.5, r128). Not faster than the baseline on compression; included as an optimal-ratio niche project. GitHub is a mirror, the main repository is the author's site (so last-commit date may understate activity).
